For the protection of genomic data from being used against

B. A PROPOSED HOLISTIC INTEGRATED PRECISION
MEDICINE FRAMEWORK
To address the unresolved challenges of PM, more informat-
ics approaches are required to be designed. We designed a
futuristic framework (Figure 8), by incorporating functions
covering the most needed areas of PM implementation. The
framework is a high-level demonstration of modules, such as
primary analysis, secondary analysis connected with knowl-
edge management, and data analytics that produce knowledge
and data services. These services are provisioned to use by
different stakeholders and organizations that include hospi-
tals, pharmacies, and laboratories. The framework has also a
provision for security and privacy functions to access to the
individuals’ data through adequate authentication, authoriza-
tion, and access policies.
The primary analysis module is designed to acquire diverse
data from different input sources, which include clinical data,
molecular and -omic data, sensory data, environmental data,
and published literature data. At this stage, the data is pre-
processed to filter-out the undesirable data items through the
application of different natural language preprocessing and
other statistical techniques. The primary analysis module uti-
lizes the support of multiple tools particularly -omic data pre-
processing tools, such as GMAP, BWA, GATK, and others.
The secondary analysis module analyzes the data received
as an outcome from the primary analysis. Some parts of
the data need to be integrated for a combined analysis, and
others may be analyzed independently. One of the important
activities is to find correlations among various data items,
such as among the genes and how they are related while
studying a disease occurrence due the genes mutations. Sim-
ilarly, it takes care of the correlation between genotypes and
phenotypes to study the relationships of clinical factors and
gene mutations. The analyzed data is stored as an internal
storage for further processing, and it is provided to the exter-
nal entities as a service.
There are two modules on the top of the secondary anal-
ysis, which include knowledge management and data ana-
lytics. Both modules utilize the analyzed data generated at
the secondary analysis. The knowledge management mod-
ule constructs KBs by creating, maintaining, and validating
knowledge rules from the analyzed data. Based on this knowl-
edge, various knowledge services, such as clinical decision
support services can be produced. Similarly, the data analytics
module targets designing models for descriptive, predictive,
and prescriptive services. The analytical models generate data
visualization services to present data in graphs, charts, and
other statistical modes of presentations.

IX. CONCLUSION
Both medical professionals and informatics researchers
across the globe have started device computational infras-
tructural solutions to address the need of timely and precise
decision about patients’ health issues. It is a high time for
both the informatics community and the medical community
to collaborate with each other to develop a combined effort
to achieve the common goal of better-quality patient care.
In this study, we elaborated the major areas of research and
development for the realization of PM in the perspective of
informatics. The study provides a lot of attention to cover
the important aspects and requirements to establish the PM
program. We explained the need of the coexistence of EBM
and PM by bridging the gap between them. To understand
the informatics viewpoint of how the PM is implemented,
we provided an overview of the enabling tools and techniques
in three potential areas, which include biomedical informat-
ics, clinical informatics, and participatory health informatics.
For a deeper understanding of PM, the paper offers a broad
view on how AI and big data become an integral part of PM.
We also associated the IoT paradigm with PM and uncovered
various advantages of integrating the two approaches.
In addition, this paper highlights some of the major imple-
mentation challenges in terms of computational tools, data
integration, security, standardization, and overall infrastruc-
tural solutions that are required to implement PM. Finally,
we proposed an integrated holistic framework for PM to over-
come the existing limitations. In summary, the outcomes of
this study are expected to be beneficial for the researchers and
the professionals working in the area of medical informatics.
An array of future works is required to see PM in its
maximum potentials. Of the essentials, the low computational
complexity solutions for molecular and -omics data analysis
appears as a big challenge. Processing and mining heteroge-
neous datasets such as omics, imaging, clinical data required
for associated predictions also requires a large volume of
research works. Furthermore, introducing secure mechanisms
to protect genomic data from being maliciously used is still
an open issue.

# Annotated Bibliography

## Source
Afzal, M., Islam, S. M. R., Hussain, M., & Lee, S. (2020). Precision medicine informatics: Principles, prospects, and challenges. *IEEE Access*, 8, 13593-13612. https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2020.2965955

## Annotation

This comprehensive review article provides a holistic examination of precision medicine (PM) from an informatics perspective, addressing the technological infrastructure needed to support individualized healthcare approaches. The authors systematically survey the current state of PM informatics across three key domains: bioinformatics, clinical informatics, and participatory health informatics.

**Key Contributions:**
The paper makes several significant contributions to the field. First, it bridges the conceptual gap between evidence-based medicine (EBM) and precision medicine, arguing for their coexistence rather than replacement. The authors propose specific reconciliation strategies and highlight how both approaches can complement each other in clinical practice. Second, the review provides an extensive catalog of enabling tools and technologies, from genomic analysis platforms like GMAP and GATK to clinical decision support systems and consumer health applications. Third, the authors examine the integration of emerging technologies including big data analytics, artificial intelligence, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices in precision medicine workflows.

**Methodology:**
The authors employed the PRISMA methodology for their literature review, searching Web of Science and PubMed databases with specific inclusion/exclusion criteria focused on informatics aspects rather than purely clinical or biological perspectives. This approach resulted in a comprehensive but focused analysis of the computational and technological challenges in PM implementation.

**Major Findings:**
The review identifies several critical implementation challenges including data complexity and volume, integration of heterogeneous data types, privacy concerns, and the need for standardization. The authors highlight that current clinical decision support systems require significant redesign to accommodate the multi-dimensional data requirements of PM, including genomic, clinical, environmental, and lifestyle data.

**Framework Contribution:**
A notable strength of this work is the proposed "holistic integrated precision medicine framework" that addresses identified limitations in current approaches. This framework incorporates primary and secondary analysis modules, knowledge management systems, and data analytics capabilities while emphasizing security and privacy considerations.

**Limitations and Critical Assessment:**
While comprehensive, the review has some limitations. The focus on informatics tools may not fully address the clinical workflow integration challenges that practitioners face. Additionally, some of the technological optimism around AI and big data integration may underestimate the practical barriers to implementation, particularly in resource-constrained healthcare settings. The proposed framework, while conceptually sound, lacks empirical validation or implementation details that would facilitate practical adoption.

**Relevance for Current Practice:**
This article serves as a valuable resource for researchers, healthcare informaticists, and computer scientists working on precision medicine implementations. The systematic categorization of tools and identification of standardization efforts provides practical guidance for technology selection and system design. However, practitioners should be aware that the field continues to evolve rapidly, and some of the specific tools and platforms mentioned may have been superseded by newer alternatives since publication.

**Research Implications:**
The authors identify several areas for future research, including the development of low computational complexity solutions for genomic data analysis, improved methods for integrating heterogeneous datasets, and enhanced privacy protection mechanisms. These research directions remain highly relevant for advancing the field toward practical, scalable precision medicine implementations.

**Overall Assessment:**
This review provides a comprehensive and well-structured analysis of precision medicine informatics that effectively bridges technical and clinical perspectives. While some of the technological optimism may need tempering with practical implementation realities, the systematic approach and comprehensive coverage make it a valuable reference for understanding the current state and future challenges of precision medicine from an informatics standpoint.

The authors argue that precision medicine isn't meant to replace evidence-based medicine but work alongside it, and they spend considerable time explaining how these two approaches can complement each other. They organize their analysis around three key informatics areas: bioinformatics (tools for analyzing genetic data like GMAP and GATK), clinical informatics (electronic health records and decision support systems), and participatory health informatics (wearable devices and patient-generated data). A major contribution is their proposed framework for integrating all these different data sources while maintaining privacy and security.

The paper reads more like a comprehensive survey than original research, which makes sense given their systematic literature review approach using PRISMA methodology. The authors clearly know the field well and do a solid job cataloguing existing tools and identifying gaps. I found their discussion of how IoT devices and AI could enhance precision medicine particularly interesting, especially their example of using sensors to improve deep brain stimulation therapy for Parkinson's patients. However, some of their enthusiasm for emerging technologies feels a bit overstated - they don't spend enough time on the practical barriers to implementing these systems in real healthcare settings, like cost, training, and workflow disruption.

One thing that struck me was their emphasis on data integration challenges. They point out that current clinical decision support systems aren't designed to handle genomic data alongside traditional clinical information, which creates real implementation problems. Their proposed solution makes theoretical sense, but I wondered how realistic it would be for smaller healthcare organizations to adopt such complex systems. The paper also raises important questions about data privacy that become even more critical when you're dealing with genetic information that could affect not just patients but their families.

Overall, this is a useful overview for anyone trying to understand the current state of precision medicine technology, though it's definitely written for an academic audience familiar with informatics concepts. The systematic approach and comprehensive coverage make it a solid reference, even if some of the technological optimism needs to be balanced with real-world implementation realities.

1 [General Definition: 4 pts] Explain the following terms.

space.

input.title: Comprehensive Typing App Enhancement Prompt
input.content:
# Typing Practice App Enhancement Request

## CONTEXT
I have a fully functional PyQt6 typing practice application (TypingApp.py) that teaches touch typing through progressive lessons. The app currently tracks WPM, accuracy, errors, and progress. Users can type practice text, see real-time highlighting, and advance through lessons. However, several key features are missing that would significantly improve the learning experience.

## PRIMARY OBJECTIVE
Enhance the typing practice application with three critical improvements:
1. **Backspace penalty system** (HIGH PRIORITY)
2. **Keyboard visualization with next-key highlighting**
3. **Comprehensive statistics dashboard with historical tracking**

## CURRENT STATE ANALYSIS

### What Works Well
- Lesson progression with 10 built-in lessons
- Real-time character highlighting (correct/incorrect)
- WPM and accuracy calculation
- Progress persistence via JSON
- Free practice mode with custom text import
- Best WPM tracking per lesson

### Critical Issue: Backspace Has No Penalty
Currently, users can backspace freely to correct mistakes without any consequence. This allows "cheating" by repeatedly correcting errors to achieve artificially high accuracy scores. This defeats the purpose of touch typing practice, which should encourage forward progress and muscle memory development.

## DETAILED REQUIREMENTS

### 1. BACKSPACE PENALTY SYSTEM (Must Implement First)

#### Requirement 1A: Track Backspace Usage
- Add a `backspace_count` field to the `TypingSession` dataclass
- Increment this counter every time backspace is pressed
- Display backspace count in the stats section with a new label

#### Requirement 1B: Penalize WPM for Backspaces
- Modify `_calculate_wpm()` to apply a penalty for backspaces
- Suggested formula: `effective_wpm = raw_wpm - (backspace_count * penalty_factor)`
- Use a penalty factor of 2-5 WPM per backspace (configurable)
- Never let WPM go below 0

#### Requirement 1C: Penalize Accuracy for Backspaces
- Modify `_calculate_accuracy()` to treat backspaces as additional errors
- Formula: `total_errors = mismatch_errors + extra_char_errors + (backspace_count * backspace_weight)`
- Use a backspace weight of 0.5-1.0 (configurable)

#### Requirement 1D: Optional Strict Mode
- Add a checkbox/toggle in the UI: "Strict Mode (Disable Backspace)"
- When enabled, intercept backspace key events and prevent deletion
- Show a brief visual indicator (e.g., red flash) when backspace is attempted in strict mode
- Save strict mode preference to the progress JSON

#### Requirement 1E: UI Updates
- Add backspace counter to stats section: `self.backspace_label = QLabel("Backspaces: 0")`
- Style it distinctly (e.g., orange background) to draw attention
- Show backspace count in completion message
- Update `on_completion()` to display: "Backspaces: X (penalty: -Y WPM)"

### 2. KEYBOARD VISUALIZATION

#### Requirement 2A: Virtual Keyboard Display
- Create a new `KeyboardWidget` class inheriting from `QWidget`
- Display a visual QWERTY keyboard layout below the typing input
- Use QPainter to draw keys as rounded rectangles
- Layout: 4 rows (numbers/symbols, QWERTY, ASDF, ZXCV)
- Include space bar, enter, and common punctuation

#### Requirement 2B: Next-Key Highlighting
- Highlight the NEXT key the user should press in bright green
- Determination: Compare typed text length to target text, show target[len(typed)]
- If user has typed incorrectly, highlight the CORRECT key they should have typed (in red/orange)
- Dim or gray out already-typed keys
- Reset highlighting on completion or reset

#### Requirement 2C: Finger Position Color Coding
- Color-code keys by which finger should press them:
  - Left pinky: `#e57373` (red)
  - Left ring: `#f06292` (pink)
  - Left middle: `#ba68c8` (purple)
  - Left index: `#64b5f6` (light blue)
  - Right index: `#4fc3f7` (cyan)
  - Right middle: `#4db6ac` (teal)
  - Right ring: `#81c784` (green)
  - Right pinky: `#aed581` (light green)
  - Thumbs (space): `#ffb74d` (orange)
- Add a small legend showing finger-color mapping

#### Requirement 2D: Hand Position Guide
- Optional: Show two hand outlines above the keyboard
- Highlight which finger should move for the next key

### 3. STATISTICS DASHBOARD

#### Requirement 3A: Session History Tracking
- Extend `ProgressStore` to save a list of completed sessions
- Each session record contains:
  - Timestamp (ISO format)
  - Lesson index and text index
  - Final WPM
  - Final accuracy
  - Error count
  - Backspace count
  - Duration in seconds
  - Text length
- Store as `"session_history": []` in JSON
- Limit history to last 100 sessions to prevent file bloat

#### Requirement 3B: Statistics View/Dialog
- Create a new `StatisticsDialog` (QDialog) accessible via a "View Statistics" button
- Show in a tabbed interface or scrollable panel

#### Requirement 3C: Statistics to Display
**Overview Tab:**
- Total practice sessions
- Total time practiced (hours:minutes)
- Total characters typed
- Overall average WPM
- Overall average accuracy
- Current streak (consecutive days with practice)

**Progress Tab:**
- WPM over time line chart (use matplotlib or QtCharts if available, otherwise ASCII/text representation)
- Accuracy over time line chart
- Sessions per day bar chart (last 30 days)

**Performance Tab:**
- Best WPM ever (with lesson name and date)
- Best accuracy ever
- Most practiced lesson
- Weakest lesson (lowest average WPM)

**Error Analysis Tab:**
- Most commonly mistyped keys (if tracking individual key errors)
- Average backspace count per session
- Error rate trends

#### Requirement 3D: Export Functionality
- Add "Export Statistics" button in StatisticsDialog
- Export to CSV with columns: Date, Lesson, WPM, Accuracy, Errors, Backspaces, Duration
- Use QFileDialog to let user choose save location

### 4. ADDITIONAL IMPROVEMENTS (Secondary Priority)

#### Requirement 4A: Sound Effects (Optional)
- Add subtle audio feedback using QSound or PyQt6.QtMultimedia
- Correct keystroke: soft click
- Error: gentle beep
- Completion: success chime
- Include on/off toggle in settings

#### Requirement 4B: Dark Mode Toggle
- Add "Dark Mode" checkbox in UI
- Define two color schemes (light and dark)
- Apply to all widgets dynamically
- Save preference to JSON

#### Requirement 4C: Settings Panel
- Create a settings dialog with:
  - Backspace penalty factor (slider: 0-10)
  - Backspace accuracy weight (slider: 0.0-2.0)
  - Strict mode toggle
  - Sound effects toggle
  - Dark mode toggle
  - Font size adjustment (12-24pt)
- Save all settings to progress JSON

## CONSTRAINTS

### Technical Constraints
- Must use PyQt6 (no other GUI frameworks)
- Must remain compatible with existing code structure
- Must maintain backward compatibility with existing `typing_progress.json` files
- No external dependencies beyond PyQt6 and standard library
- Should work on Windows, macOS, and Linux

### Performance Constraints
- UI must remain responsive (<16ms per frame ideally)
- Keyboard visualization should not lag typing input
- Statistics calculations should be near-instantaneous (<100ms)

### UX Constraints
- New features should not clutter the main interface
- Statistics dialog should be separate window/dialog
- Keyboard visualization should be toggleable (show/hide)
- All new features must have tooltips explaining their purpose

## IMPLEMENTATION APPROACH

### Phase 1: Backspace System (Do This First)
1. Modify `TypingSession` dataclass to add backspace tracking
2. Add event filter or keyPressEvent override to detect backspace
3. Update `_calculate_wpm()` and `_calculate_accuracy()` with penalties
4. Add UI label for backspace count
5. Implement strict mode checkbox and logic
6. Test thoroughly with various scenarios

### Phase 2: Keyboard Visualization
1. Create `KeyboardWidget` class with QPainter rendering
2. Define key positions and sizes programmatically
3. Implement next-key highlighting logic
4. Add finger color-coding
5. Integrate into main UI (below typing input or in a dock)
6. Add show/hide toggle

### Phase 3: Statistics Dashboard
1. Extend `ProgressStore` to save session history
2. Create `StatisticsDialog` class
3. Implement data aggregation functions
4. Create basic text-based statistics display
5. Add CSV export functionality
6. (Optional) Add charting if time permits

### Phase 4: Polish & Settings
1. Create settings dialog
2. Implement theme switching
3. Add sound effects if desired
4. Add tooltips and help text
5. Final testing and bug fixes

## CODE STYLE & PATTERNS

### Follow Existing Patterns
- Use type hints for all function signatures
- Use dataclasses for data structures
- Follow existing naming conventions (snake_case for methods, PascalCase for classes)
- Add docstrings to all new methods
- Use `QTimer.singleShot()` for delayed actions
- Block signals during programmatic changes with `blockSignals(True/False)`

### Error Handling
- Use try-except for file operations
- Provide fallback behavior for missing/corrupted data
- Don't crash on invalid user input

### Testing Considerations
- Ensure backspace penalty doesn't break with edge cases (0 typed chars, 0 time elapsed)
- Test keyboard visualization with special characters
- Verify statistics calculations are accurate
- Test with corrupted progress JSON files

## EXPECTED OUTPUT

### Deliverables
1. **Modified TypingApp.py** with all three primary features implemented
2. **New KeyboardWidget class** (can be in same file or separate module)
3. **New StatisticsDialog class** (can be in same file or separate module)
4. **Updated typing_progress.json schema** with session history
5. **Code comments** explaining key algorithmic decisions (especially penalty calculations)

### Success Criteria
- [ ] Backspace key presses are tracked and penalize WPM/accuracy
- [ ] Strict mode successfully disables backspace
- [ ] Virtual keyboard displays and highlights next key correctly
- [ ] Statistics dialog shows accurate historical data
- [ ] CSV export works and contains all relevant fields
- [ ] No regressions in existing functionality
- [ ] Code follows existing style and patterns
- [ ] All new features are properly integrated into UI

## EXAMPLES

### Example 1: Backspace Penalty Calculation
```python
# Current typing state:
# - User has typed 50 characters in 10 seconds
# - 45 characters are correct, 5 are errors
# - User pressed backspace 8 times

raw_wpm = (50 / 5) / (10 / 60) = 60 WPM
backspace_penalty = 8 * 3 = 24 WPM
effective_wpm = 60 - 24 = 36 WPM

raw_accuracy = (45 / 50) * 100 = 90%
backspace_errors = 8 * 0.5 = 4 additional errors
effective_accuracy = (45 / (50 + 4)) * 100 = 83.3%
```

### Example 2: Session History Entry
```json
{
  "session_history": [
    {
      "timestamp": "2025-01-15T14:32:18",
      "lesson_index": 3,
      "text_index": 1,
      "wpm": 45,
      "accuracy": 94.5,
      "errors": 3,
      "backspaces": 2,
      "duration_seconds": 28.4,
      "text_length": 67
    }
  ]
}
```

### Example 3: Keyboard Key Highlighting
```python
# If user should type 'a' next:
def get_next_key_to_highlight(self) -> str:
    typed_len = len(self.session.typed_text)
    target_len = len(self.current_target_text)
    
    if typed_len >= target_len:
        return ""  # Completed
    
    return self.current_target_text[typed_len]

# In KeyboardWidget.paintEvent():
next_key = self.app.get_next_key_to_highlight()
if next_key.upper() == 'A':
    # Draw 'A' key with bright green highlight
    painter.setBrush(QColor("#4CAF50"))
```

## QUESTIONS TO RESOLVE
Before starting implementation, please confirm:
1. Should backspace penalty be configurable, or use fixed values?
2. Should keyboard visualization be always visible, or toggleable?
3. Do you want simple text statistics, or should I attempt charting?
4. Any specific visual design preferences for the keyboard?
5. Should strict mode be per-lesson setting or global?

## ADDITIONAL CONTEXT
This app is designed to help users learn touch typing systematically. The backspace penalty is crucial because it teaches users to type forward with confidence rather than constantly correcting. The keyboard visualization helps beginners learn key positions without looking at their physical keyboard. Statistics help users track their improvement over time, which is motivating.

---

**Please implement these enhancements in order of priority (backspace system first), maintaining code quality and the existing architecture. Ask clarifying questions if any requirements are ambiguous.**

summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The user was working on a personal cybersecurity project called "ThreatStream-lite," a threat intelligence dashboard built with FastAPI backend and web frontend. They initially asked about using Bash commands in PowerShell, learning about built-in aliases and the differences between PowerShell's `-Recurse` parameter versus Bash's `-R` flag. The conversation then shifted to troubleshooting a PowerShell script that filtered required software against installed programs using `Where-Object` and regex matching, which the user revealed was from setting up WAMP server for web development.

The main technical challenge involved integrating real threat intelligence data from CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities feed into their dashboard. The user was experiencing API connectivity issues where their endpoint returned no data. chat_messages.text:
Yes, you can use many Bash commands in PowerShell, but with some important caveats:

## Built-in Aliases

PowerShell includes built-in aliases for common Bash commands that map to PowerShell cmdlets:
- `ls` → `Get-ChildItem`
- `cd` → `Set-Location`
- `pwd` → `Get-Location`
- `cat` → `Get-Content`
- `cp` → `Copy-Item`
- `mv` → `Move-Item`
- `rm` → `Remove-Item`
- `clear` → `Clear-Host`

These work out of the box, though they use PowerShell's underlying functionality.

## Limitations

Some differences to be aware of:
- **Syntax differences**: Flags and parameters often differ (e.g., `ls -la` won't work exactly the same)
- **Output objects**: PowerShell returns objects, not text streams like Bash
- **Piping**: Works differently since you're piping objects, not text
- **Not all commands**: Many Bash-specific commands (`grep`, `awk`, `sed`) aren't available unless you install them separately

## Using Actual Bash Commands

If you want real Bash command behavior, you have a few options:
1. **Install Git Bash or WSL** - provides actual Bash utilities
2. **Install GNU utilities** via tools like Chocolatey or Scoop
3. **Use WSL directly** - run `wsl` or `bash` to enter a Linux environment

For most basic navigation and file operations, the PowerShell aliases work fine. For more complex scripting or if you need exact Bash behavior, WSL is your best bet.

chat_messages.text: What does ls -R do?

content.text: What does ls -R do?

chat_messages.text:
`ls -R` performs a **recursive listing** - it lists all files and directories in the current directory and then descends into each subdirectory, listing their contents as well, continuing recursively through the entire directory tree.

## Example output:
```
.:
folder1  folder2  file.txt

./folder1:
subfolder  file1.txt

./folder1/subfolder:
file2.txt

./folder2:
file3.txt
```

## In PowerShell:

The alias `ls -R` **won't work** in PowerShell because `-R` isn't a valid parameter for `Get-ChildItem`.

Instead, use:
```powershell
ls -Recurse
# or
Get-ChildItem -Recurse
```

This gives you the recursive behavior you're looking for. You can also use `-Depth` to limit how deep it goes:
```powershell
ls -Recurse -Depth 2
```

So while PowerShell has the `ls` alias, the flags are different - it uses `-Recurse` instead of `-R`.

chat_messages.text:
This PowerShell command filters the `$required` collection to find items that are **not** present in `$installed.DisplayName`.

## Breaking it down:

1. **`$required |`** - Pipes each item from the `$required` array through the pipeline

2. **`Where-Object { ... }`** - Filters objects based on the condition inside the script block

3. **`$req = $_;`** - Stores the current pipeline object in `$req` for easier reference
   - `$_` is the automatic variable representing the current object in the pipeline

4. **`-not ($installed.DisplayName -match $req)`** - The filter condition:
   - `$installed.DisplayName` - Accesses the DisplayName property (likely an array)
   - `-match $req` - Tests if any DisplayName matches the current required item (uses regex matching)
   - `-not` - Negates the result, so it returns `$true` when there's **no match**

## What it does:
Returns all items from `$required` that are NOT found in `$installed.DisplayName`.

## Example:
```powershell
$required = @("Git", "Python", "Node")
$installed = @(
    [PSCustomObject]@{DisplayName="Git"},
    [PSCustomObject]@{DisplayName="VSCode"}
)

$missing = $required | Where-Object { $req = $_; -not ($installed.DisplayName -match $req) }
# Result: @("Python", "Node")
```

This is commonly used to check for missing dependencies or software that needs to be installed.

# python
from pathlib import Path
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.staticfiles import StaticFiles
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import List
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
import random, requests

app = FastAPI(title="ThreatStream Lite API")

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"],
    allow_methods=["GET"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)

# Compute `src/web` relative to this file and mount it
WEB_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "web"
if not WEB_DIR.exists():
    raise RuntimeError(f"Static directory `{WEB_DIR}` not found. Run from project root or create `src/web`.")
app.mount("/", StaticFiles(directory=str(WEB_DIR), html=True), name="web")


# --- MODEL ---
class Alert(BaseModel):
    id: str
    title: str
    severity: str
    source: str
    date: datetime
    status: str


# --- MOCK DATA GENERATOR (fallback) ---
SOURCES = ["CISA", "NVD", "US-CERT", "OTX"]
SEVERITY = ["critical", "high", "medium", "low"]
STATUS = ["Investigating", "Mitigated", "Under Review", "Published"]


def rand_item(arr): return random.choice(arr)


def days_ago_random(max_days: int) -> datetime:
    days = random.randint(0, max_days)
    hours = random.randint(0, 23)
    minutes = random.randint(0, 59)
    return datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(days=days, hours=hours, minutes=minutes)


def title_for(sev: str) -> str:
    verbs = {"critical": "Exploited", "high": "Vulnerability", "medium": "Advisory", "low": "Notice"}
    targets = ["OpenSSL", "Linux kernel", "Windows RPC", "Cisco ASA", "Fortinet", "Apache HTTPD", "Nginx", "Kubernetes"]
    return f"{verbs.get(sev, 'Advisory')} in {rand_item(targets)} ({sev.upper()})"


def generate_mock(count: int = 80, within_days: int = 30) -> List[Alert]:
    items = []
    for i in range(count):
        sev = rand_item(SEVERITY)
        items.append(
            Alert(
                id=f"ALRT-{str(i + 1).zfill(4)}",
                title=title_for(sev),
                severity=sev,
                source=rand_item(SOURCES),
                date=days_ago_random(within_days),
                status=rand_item(STATUS),
            )
        )
    return sorted(items, key=lambda x: x.date, reverse=True)


ALL_ALERTS = generate_mock(60, 45)

# --- LIVE DATA SOURCE ---
CISA_FEED = "https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json"


# --- ROUTE ---
@app.get("/api/alerts", response_model=List[Alert])
def get_alerts(since_days: int = 30, limit: int = 500):
    # Corrected cutoff to compare against the start of the day
    cutoff_date = datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(days=since_days)
    cutoff = cutoff_date.replace(hour=0, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)
    alerts: List[Alert] = []

    try:
        res = requests.get(CISA_FEED, timeout=8)
        if res.ok:
            data = res.json().get("vulnerabilities", [])
            for i, v in enumerate(data):  # Removed limit slice here to filter all by date first
                alerts.append(Alert(
                    id=f"CISA-{v.get('cveID', i)}",
                    title=f"{v.get('vendorProject', 'Unknown')} - {v.get('product', 'N/A')}",
                    severity="critical",
                    source="CISA",
                    date=datetime.strptime(v.get("dateAdded"), "%Y-%m-%d"),
                    status="Published"
                ))

        # Filter by date first, then apply the limit
        alerts = [a for a in alerts if a.date >= cutoff]
        # Sort by date descending before limiting
        alerts = sorted(alerts, key=lambda x: x.date, reverse=True)[:limit]

    except Exception as e:
        print("⚠️ CISA feed failed:", e)

    # fallback if feed failed or empty
    if not alerts:
        alerts = [a for a in ALL_ALERTS if a.date >= cutoff][:limit]

    return alerts


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn

    uvicorn.run("src.api.main:app", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000, reload=True)

input.content:
from pathlib import Path
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.staticfiles import StaticFiles
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import List
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
import random, requests

app = FastAPI(title="ThreatStream Lite API")

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"],
    allow_methods=["GET"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)


# --- MODEL ---
class Alert(BaseModel):
    id: str
    title: str
    severity: str
    source: str
    date: datetime
    status: str


# --- MOCK DATA GENERATOR (fallback) ---
SOURCES = ["CISA", "NVD", "US-CERT", "OTX"]
SEVERITY = ["critical", "high", "medium", "low"]
STATUS = ["Investigating", "Mitigated", "Under Review", "Published"]


def rand_item(arr): return random.choice(arr)


def days_ago_random(max_days: int) -> datetime:
    days = random.randint(0, max_days)
    hours = random.randint(0, 23)
    minutes = random.randint(0, 59)
    return datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(days=days, hours=hours, minutes=minutes)


def title_for(sev: str) -> str:
    verbs = {"critical": "Exploited", "high": "Vulnerability", "medium": "Advisory", "low": "Notice"}
    targets = ["OpenSSL", "Linux kernel", "Windows RPC", "Cisco ASA", "Fortinet", "Apache HTTPD", "Nginx", "Kubernetes"]
    return f"{verbs.get(sev, 'Advisory')} in {rand_item(targets)} ({sev.upper()})"


def generate_mock(count: int = 80, within_days: int = 30) -> List[Alert]:
    items = []
    for i in range(count):
        sev = rand_item(SEVERITY)
        items.append(
            Alert(
                id=f"ALRT-{str(i + 1).zfill(4)}",
                title=title_for(sev),
                severity=sev,
                source=rand_item(SOURCES),
                date=days_ago_random(within_days),
                status=rand_item(STATUS),
            )
        )
    return sorted(items, key=lambda x: x.date, reverse=True)


ALL_ALERTS = generate_mock(60, 45)

# --- LIVE DATA SOURCE ---
CISA_FEED = "https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json"


# --- API ROUTE (MUST BE BEFORE STATIC MOUNT) ---
@app.get("/api/alerts", response_model=List[Alert])
def get_alerts(since_days: int = 30, limit: int = 500):
    cutoff_date = datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(days=since_days)
    cutoff = cutoff_date.replace(hour=0, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)
    alerts: List[Alert] = []

    try:
        print(f"🔍 Fetching from {CISA_FEED}...")
        res = requests.get(CISA_FEED, timeout=8)
        print(f"📡 Status code: {res.status_code}")
        
        if res.ok:
            data = res.json().get("vulnerabilities", [])
            print(f"📊 Found {len(data)} total vulnerabilities")
            
            for i, v in enumerate(data):
                try:
                    date_str = v.get("dateAdded")
                    if not date_str:
                        continue
                    
                    parsed_date = datetime.strptime(date_str, "%Y-%m-%d")
                    
                    alerts.append(Alert(
                        id=f"CISA-{v.get('cveID', f'UNK-{i}')}",
                        title=f"{v.get('vendorProject', 'Unknown')} - {v.get('product', 'N/A')} - {v.get('vulnerabilityName', 'Vulnerability')}",
                        severity="critical",
                        source="CISA",
                        date=parsed_date,
                        status="Published"
                    ))
                except Exception as parse_err:
                    print(f"⚠️ Failed to parse vulnerability {i}: {parse_err}")
                    continue

            print(f"✅ Parsed {len(alerts)} alerts before filtering")
            
        else:
            print(f"❌ API returned status {res.status_code}")

        # Filter by date first, then apply the limit
        alerts = [a for a in alerts if a.date >= cutoff]
        alerts = sorted(alerts, key=lambda x: x.date, reverse=True)[:limit]
        print(f"📋 Returning {len(alerts)} alerts after filtering")

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"❌ CISA feed failed: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
        import traceback
        traceback.print_exc()

    # fallback if feed failed or empty
    if not alerts:
        print("⚠️ Using mock data fallback")
        alerts = [a for a in ALL_ALERTS if a.date >= cutoff][:limit]

    return alerts


# --- STATIC FILES MOUNT (MUST BE LAST) ---
WEB_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "web"
if not WEB_DIR.exists():
    raise RuntimeError(f"Static directory `{WEB_DIR}` not found. Run from project root or create `src/web`.")
app.mount("/", StaticFiles(directory=str(WEB_DIR), html=True), name="web")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn
    uvicorn.run("src.api.main:app", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000, reload=True)

import sys

from PyQt6.QtCore import Qt

    painter.drawRoundedRect(pixmap.rect(), 28, 28)

    painter.setPen(QPen(QColor("#ffffff")))
    painter.setFont(QFont("Montserrat", 64, QFont.Weight.Bold))
    painter.drawText(pixmap.rect(), Qt.AlignmentFlag.AlignCenter, "T")

    painter.end()
    return QIcon(pixmap)


def main() -> None:
    app = QApplication(sys.argv)
    app.setStyle("Fusion")
    app.setWindowIcon(build_window_icon())

chat_messages.text:
Building an NES emulator is an excellent project that will teach you tons about low-level programming, CPU architecture, and how hardware really works. Here's a solid roadmap:

**Foundation Phase**

Start by understanding the NES architecture. Read through the nesdev wiki thoroughly - it's the bible for this project. Focus on understanding the 6502 CPU, memory mapping, and how the different components interact. You'll want to set up your development environment with a language that gives you good control - C, C++, or Rust are popular choices.

**CPU Implementation**

Begin with the 6502 CPU core since everything else depends on it. Implement the instruction set one opcode at a time, starting with the most common ones like LDA, STA, and the arithmetic operations. Write tests for each instruction using known test ROMs like nestest. Get the CPU passing nestest before moving forward - this saves you from debugging nightmares later.

**Memory and Mappers**

Implement the memory management unit and address decoding. Start with mapper 0 (NROM) since it's the simplest - games like Donkey Kong and Super Mario Bros use it. You can add more complex mappers like MMC1 and MMC3 later once everything else works.

**PPU (Picture Processing Unit)**

This is the hardest part. Break it down into rendering the background first, then sprites. Implement scanline rendering, understanding how the PPU draws one line at a time. Handle sprite zero hit detection and the various PPU registers. Start by just getting something on screen, even if the colors are wrong.

**APU and Controllers**

Add the Audio Processing Unit for sound - this can be simplified initially. Implement controller input handling so you can actually play the games. The standard NES controller is straightforward with just 8 buttons.

**Testing and Refinement**

Test with progressively more complex games. Start with simple mapper 0 games, then move to games that stress different systems. Fix timing issues, which will be ongoing. Consider adding debugging tools like a CPU step debugger and PPU viewer.

**Enhancement Phase**

Once games are playable, you can add save states, rewind functionality, debugger improvements, or even netplay if you're ambitious.

The whole project typically takes a few months of focused work. The CPU might take 2-3 weeks, the PPU another month or more. Would you like me to dive deeper into any particular component?

```
I want to build an NES emulator from scratch in [C++/Rust/your preferred language]. This is a learning project to understand low-level system architecture and emulation.

For the first phase, I need help setting up the foundation and beginning the 6502 CPU implementation:

1. PROJECT STRUCTURE:
- Set up a clean project structure with appropriate directories (src, include, tests, roms, etc.)
- Configure a build system (CMake/Cargo/etc.)
- Set up a testing framework for CPU instruction verification

2. INITIAL 6502 CPU CORE:
- Create the CPU struct/class with registers (A, X, Y, SP, PC, status flags)
- Implement the fetch-decode-execute cycle
- Start with these essential opcodes first:
  * LDA (Load Accumulator): 0xA9 (immediate), 0xA5 (zero page), 0xAD (absolute)
  * STA (Store Accumulator): 0x85 (zero page), 0x8D (absolute)
  * LDX, LDY (Load X/Y registers)
  * Basic arithmetic: ADC, SBC
  * Transfers: TAX, TAY, TXA, TYA
  * Stack operations: PHA, PLA, PHP, PLP
  * JMP, JSR, RTS
  * Branch instructions: BEQ, BNE, BCS, BCC

3. MEMORY SYSTEM:
- Implement a simple memory bus (64KB address space)
- Basic read/write functions
- Placeholder for mapper implementation later

4. TESTING SETUP:
- Show me how to structure CPU tests
- Provide a few example tests for the implemented opcodes
- Explain how I'll integrate nestest.nes later

Please provide well-commented code with explanations of the 6502 architecture decisions. I want to understand WHY things work this way, not just copy code. Include cycle counting from the start since timing will matter later.

Start with the project structure and CPU core skeleton, then we'll implement opcodes incrementally.
```

This prompt is structured to get Opus thinking deeply about the architecture while being specific enough to get actionable code. The "thinking" model will reason through the design decisions before generating code, which is perfect for a complex project like this.

chat_messages.text:
**Hold off on deploying multiple agents for this.** Here's why:

For the initial foundation phase, you want a single coherent architecture and consistent design decisions. Multiple agents working simultaneously could give you:
- Conflicting implementations of the same components
- Inconsistent coding styles and patterns
- Architectural decisions that don't mesh well together
- More confusion than productivity when you're still learning the domain

**Better approach:**

Use a single agent session to build the foundation incrementally. Work through the CPU implementation one step at a time, testing as you go. This lets you actually learn and understand what's happening rather than just assembling pieces.

**When multi-agent makes sense:**

Once you have a working CPU core and basic architecture established, THEN you could parallelize:
- One agent working on PPU implementation
- Another on APU/sound system  
- Another on additional mapper support
- One building debugging tools

But even then, you'd need to integrate everything carefully and resolve conflicts.

**My recommendation:**

Start with one focused Cursor session. Get the CPU working and passing nestest. Once you deeply understand your own codebase and have that solid foundation, then consider splitting off independent components to other agents. The learning value comes from building it sequentially and debugging it yourself.

This is a learning project - the process matters as much as the result. You'll gain way more CS knowledge from wrestling with the problems than from managing agent outputs.

The Software Emulation of the NES Console

                   Author: qeed

--------------------[Table of Contents]-----------------------------------
	I.    Introduction
	II.   ROMs/INES/UNIF
	III.  CPU (Central Processing Unit)
	IV.   PPU (Picture Processing Unit)
	V.    APU (Audio Processing Unit)
	VI.   Miscellaneous
	VII.  Thanks
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

			I. Introduction

	This document is intended to introduce the basics of the NES 
architecture, with the main focus on how to emulate such a console on the
software side. Supplementary links will be provided at the end for 
anyone who wanted the hardware side of the NES. The code and optimization 
tricks presented in this article will be mainly C and assembly, 
although it should be easily ported to other languages. The information
in this article will try to cover the base NES hardware, 
and only the base. The peripherals will be provided external links 
for those who wish to learn more. The reasons I wanted to write this 
document was to cover all the latest information that was discovered
over the years about the NES. Many of documents about the NES nowadays
are sorely outdated, and some even outright wrong. I want to give thanks
to the people such as Brad Taylor, blargg, kevtris,  loopy, 
quietust, disch, and the all the other members of the NESDEV community 
for writing about and  discovering all the new things about the NES. 
Emulation couldn't have been this accurate without all of 
your contributions! This is really a compilation of methods/info used and
found by others. I made sure to give where credit is due here depending 
on who told me about it/where I found it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

			II. ROMs/INES/UNIF

	First and foremost, the main use of console emulators besides the 
intellectual pursuit is to play video games. ROMs are the back up images
you get from the game board that has been dumped by a cartridge reader, 
for the NES, the main dumper is the CopyNES. Now due to the NES limited
hardware, the NES game cartridge contains extra hardware that extends the 
capabilities of the NES hardware, such as sound chips, RAM, 
and banks that allow more ROM space for code. These extra hardware add-ons
can be controlled by writing to memory-mapped registers, and each hardware
cartridge had different registers. Of this fact, the INES header was born.

	The INES header was a format invented by Marat Fayzullin 
to classify the type of cartridge one would be reading when 
opening the ROM file. The current INES specification is 16 bytes of 
header file, following then the optional trainer if the file has one, 
a small chunk of code for a cheat screen mainly, 
the PRG-ROM, the game code, and then the CHR-ROM, the graphics data, 
at the end there is also the playchoice (8kb of hint screen) 
at the end after CHR-ROM if the flag for it is set.

	The UNIF format was created later to provide more accurate information 
about the game cartridge, using full board names of the cartridge instead 
of assigning a number for it, it is also a chunked format based, allowing 
alot more flexibility in updating the standard, though UNIF never widely 
caught on, and most dumped games uses the INES header format, so for 
emulating the NES, implementing INES should be sufficient for most games. 
The game cartridge are classified with "mapper" numbers in INES and 
board names in UNIF.

+++++++++++++++++++++++++INES header++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

	Here is the INES data format taken from nesdevwiki:

header[0, 3] = "NES\x1a" the header string identifying a INES ROM. the 0x1A
			   is the MS-DOS end of line terminator.

header[4] = The number of PRG-ROM inside the file (0x4000 * header[4]) 
			bytes.

header[5] = The number of CHR-ROM inside the file (0x2000 * header[5]) 
            bytes.

header[6] = 
76543210
||||||||
||||+||+- 0xx0: horizontal mirroring; 0xx1: vertical mirroring; 
		  1xxx: four-screen mirroring
|||| |+-- 1: SRAM in CPU $6000-$7FFF, if present, is battery backed
|||| +--- 1: 512-byte trainer at $7000-$71FF (stored before PRG data)
++++----- Lower nybble of mapper number

header[7] = 
76543210
||||  ||
||||  |+- VS Unisystem
||||  +-- PlayChoice-10 (8KB of Hint Screen data stored after CHR data)
++++----- Upper nybble of mapper number

header[8] = Size of PRG RAM in 8 KB units 
			(Value 0 implies 8 KB for compatibility; see PRG RAM circuit) 

header[9] = 
76543210
||||||||
|||||||+- TV system (0: NTSC; 1: PAL)
+++++++-- Reserved, set to zero
Not alot of emulator adheres to this, and many if not all
ROMs dumped do not use this flag.

header[10] =
76543210
  ||  ||
  ||  ++- TV system (0: NTSC; 2: PAL; 1/3: dual compatible)
  |+----- SRAM in CPU $6000-$7FFF is 0: present; 1: not present
  +------ 0: Board has no bus conflicts; 1: Board has bus conflicts
header[10] is unofficial from the INES spec, if you want to adhere
to the spec, treat header[10] as unused (zero-filled).

header[11,15] are unused (zero-filled).

	After this, there is a 512 bytes trainer if bit 2 of header 6 is set,
and then header[4] * 16384 bytes of PRG-ROM, 
then header[5] * 8192 of CHR-ROM, and 8192 bytes of PlayChoice-10 data 
at after the CHR-ROM.

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

++++++++++++++++++++++UNIF Header Format++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

	Here is the UNIF header format taken from nesdevwiki:
header[0, 3] = "UNIF" identifer

header[4, 7] = What version of the UNIF we are dealing with

header[8, 31] = Reserved.

From then there is string identfiers saying what data comes next
here is the chunk idenfitier format.

00-03: Chunk ID string, ASCII text
04-07: Chunk data length, DWORD
08-..: Chunk data 

Here is the string identifier in alphabetical format:

"BATR"
Length=1 byte
Revision=5
Recommended in file
	Indicates that the board contains a battery used to 
preserve the contents of its expansion RAM.

"CCK#" where # is a number
Length=4 bytes
Revision=5
Optional in the file
	"CCK0" to "CCKF" contains CRC32 checksums which
verifies if the data has been dumped properly.

"CHR#" where # is a number
Length=variable size
Revision=4
"CHR0" is required, all others are optional, only if the game has CHR-ROM.
